newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Aid workers say east Zaire airport falls to Tutsis.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers say east Zaire airport falls to Tutsis.

text.p: Ethnic Zairean Tutsis fighting Zaire's troops were reported to have seized the airport in the eastern Zairean town of Uvira on Friday and cut off satellite and radio communications, Western aid workers said.
The reports could not be confirmed independently and there have been no credible witness accounts of the fighting so far.

But the aid workers in Geneva, citing field reports, said Tutsi Banyamulenge fighters, resisting Zairean attempts to force them back to Rwanda, took the Kiliba airport in Uvira on the shores of Lake Tanganyika and many people were fleeing the town.

There were unconfirmed reports that Uvira town itself had fallen, as well as a second town near Goma, a region to the north home to 700,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled after 1994's Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis.
One Western aid source in the region said Uvira was reported to be deserted and that many people were heading south.
Zairean troops, many of them unpaid for months and more interested in looting than in fighting, had fled the town, aid workers said.
"Uvira is empty. People are moving out and heading south," said one aid worker.

Fighting in the region broke out after ethnic Banyamulenge Tutsis, who came to Zaire as long ago as the end of the 18th century, resisted Zairean attempts to drive them from their land and force them back into Rwanda.

Earlier, aid workers reported heavy fighting in Uvira and said a local U.N. radio operator in the city reported on Thursday night he would stop transmitting as the rebels were about to take the area. He then went off the air.
Aid workers said they had lost telephone and radio contact with their local staff in Uvira earlier on Friday. Aid agencies have evacuated international staff from the town.
Reports say the Tutsi resistance appears more coordinated in recent days.
Zaire, whose stricken president Mobutu Sese Seko is undergoing cancer treatment in Switzerland since August, has accused Rwanda of invading eastern Zaire. Rwanda has denied the charge.

Extremist Hutu militia among the refugees have kept the military threat alive with forays into Rwanda from sprawling camps administered by the U.N. and aid agencies. Rwanda has repeatedly urged the U.N. to close down the camps.
Rwanda's minority Tutsi rulers, who took power after the genocide of more than half a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus, feel persecuted, outnumbered and surrounded by majority Hutus.

Some members of Rwanda's Tutsi-led army say privately they are prepared to take matters into their own hands. Many of the army's soldiers grew up in neighbouring Zaire, Uganda and Burundi and would be at home across the borders.
